exercise1.prompt: grades = [85, 90, 78], append 92, remove 78, print the list

hiddenCases.name: the list is changed with append and remove
hiddenCases.describe: append() to add 92 and remove() to take 78 out

exercise1.hint: append() and remove() change the list they are called on and hand back nothing. Watch what grades holds after each line rather than what the method returns.

exercise2.prompt: numbers = [5, 2, 8, 2, 1], sort it, count the 2s, print both

hiddenCases.name: sort() orders the list and count() counts the 2s
the list and the count are both printed

exercise2.hint: sort() rearranges the list itself and returns None, so assigning its result over the variable throws the list away. Sort first, then ask the list how many 2s it has.

questions.prompt: What is the value of numbers after numbers = numbers.sort()?
questions.explain: sort() rearranges the list in place and returns None, so the assignment replaces your list with None. Call numbers.sort() on its own line instead.

questions.prompt: What does [1, 2].append([3, 4]) leave the list holding?
questions.explain: append() adds exactly one item, and here that item is a list. extend() is the one that adds each element separately.

questions.prompt: Which of these change the list they are called on?
questions.explain: append() and remove() modify the list and return None. count() and index() only look at it and hand back an answer.

questions.prompt: Put these lines in order so the final list is [85, 90, 92].
questions.explain: The list has to exist before a method can be called on it, and the print has to come last or it shows a list that is not finished yet.

questions.prompt: numbers.___(2) removes the first 2 from the list, and numbers.___(2) tells you how many 2s there are.
questions.explain: remove() takes a value out and count() reports how often that value appears. Neither one takes an index.
